name: Push Notification Delivery
intent: Send a notification to a phone through the platform push service with a device token, a time to live, a collapse key and a priority, and treat delivery as best effort: the app must be able to fetch anything critical when it opens.
scenario: A sports and chat app sends 30 notifications in a day, some of them score updates. One phone is offline for 4 hours, with a time to live of 120 minutes: 28 arrive and 2 expire. With collapsing on, 2 older score updates are replaced by the newest. Separately the server sends the same 30 to 1,000 device tokens, 10% of them dead: 3,000 wasted sends without pruning, 100 with it.
problem: Your server cannot open a connection to a phone. The operating system keeps one shared connection to its vendor's push service, and your message goes through it. That brings limits you do not control: the service holds a message for an offline phone only for a time, newer messages can replace older ones, a low-priority message may wait until the device is reachable, and tokens go bad when the app is uninstalled or reinstalled. Treat a push as a guaranteed delivery and users miss messages, get stale scores in a burst, and your server keeps sending to tokens that no one owns.

howItWorks.title: The app registers and the server stores a token
howItWorks.text: When the app starts, it asks the operating system to register for push and gets back a device token from the platform's push service (APNs on iOS, FCM on Android). The app sends the token to your server, which stores it against the user. The token identifies an app installation on a device, not a person, so one user can have several, and it can change.

howItWorks.title: The server sends to the platform, not to the phone
howItWorks.text: To notify, your server makes an API call to the platform push service with the token and a payload, and the platform delivers it over the connection the phone already keeps open. A success answer means the platform accepted the message, not that the phone has shown it. If the phone is offline, the platform typically stores the message for it, within limits that differ by platform: APNs keeps only one pending notification per app on a device, usually the newest (Apple does not guarantee which when several arrive close together), while FCM on Android can hold a backlog of up to 100 non-collapsible messages per device (past that it discards them all and tells the app) plus at most four collapse keys, for four weeks unless a shorter time to live is set.

howItWorks.title: Time to live, collapse key and priority shape delivery
howItWorks.text: The time to live is how long the platform may hold an undelivered message before it drops it silently: a score from three hours ago is worthless, a calendar reminder may be worth a day. A collapse key marks messages of the same kind so a newer one replaces an older pending one, and the phone gets one score instead of ten. Priority tells the platform how urgent the message is: high priority is meant to reach a device at once and to wake it, normal priority may be deferred to save battery.

howItWorks.title: Prune tokens the platform says are invalid
howItWorks.text: When an app is uninstalled or a token is replaced, the platform eventually answers sends to the old token with an error such as unregistered or invalid. The server should treat that as final and delete the token. If it keeps sending, every notification pays for a call that cannot succeed, and with a large fleet the waste becomes most of the traffic. Retrying is right for a temporary error, never for an invalid token.

howItWorks.title: Never rely on the push alone
howItWorks.text: Delivery is best effort: messages can expire, be collapsed, be dropped when the user turns notifications off, or arrive late. So a push is a hint that something changed. The data that matters, such as a new message or an order status, must also be available from your API when the app opens or comes to the foreground, and the app should fetch what it missed. The notification system case study covers the server side of fan-out.

pros: Reaches a phone whose app is closed, without your app keeping a connection or running in the background
The platform handles holding messages for offline devices, so your server does not need a queue per phone
Time to live and collapse keys stop users from receiving a burst of outdated messages
One integration per platform covers every phone with your app installed
cons: Delivery is best effort: no guarantee that a message arrives, arrives once, or arrives on time
You depend on third-party services and on how the operating system treats notifications and battery
Users can turn notifications off per app, and many do, so push cannot be the only channel
Tokens go stale all the time, so you need to track and prune them, and there is little feedback about what the user saw
whenToUse: Telling a user about something that happened while the app is closed: a message, an order update, a reminder
Prompting the app to sync, where the push is a hint and the data comes from your API
Time-sensitive alerts, with a short time to live so that stale ones are dropped instead of arriving late
whenNotToUse: As the only copy of important data, such as a one-time code with no way to request it again
High-frequency real-time updates while the app is open, where a socket or streaming connection is the right tool
Anything that must be delivered exactly once or in a strict order
pitfalls: Putting the real content only in the notification, so a message that expired or was collapsed is gone for good
Leaving the time to live at its default for time-sensitive messages, so a stale alert shows up hours later
Never pruning tokens, so dead ones are sent to on every notification
Using high priority for everything, which a platform may eventually treat as abuse and throttle
Reading 'accepted by the platform' as 'seen by the user' in delivery metrics
Not collapsing updates of the same kind, so a phone that was offline gets a burst of old ones when it returns

roles.label: Your server
roles.description: Stores device tokens and decides what to send, with what time to live, collapse key and priority.

roles.label: Platform push service
roles.description: APNs or FCM: accepts messages, holds them for offline devices and routes them.

roles.label: Phone
roles.description: Keeps one connection to the platform, receives pushes and hands them to the app.

roles.label: Mobile app
roles.description: Registers for push and fetches data from your API when it opens.

roles.label: Your API
roles.description: The source of truth the app reads on open, so a missed push loses nothing.

quiz.question: A phone is offline for 3 hours. Score updates were sent every 10 minutes with a collapse key and a time to live of 1 hour. What does the phone typically receive when it reconnects?
options: Only the newest score update, if it is still within its time to live.
All of the updates from the last hour, in the order they were sent.
All 18 updates, because the platform keeps them until delivery.
Nothing, because collapse keys only work while the phone is online.
quiz.explanation: The collapse key makes each new score replace the pending one, so only the latest is held, and the time to live drops it if it is older than an hour. With no collapse key, FCM could deliver the whole backlog still inside the time to live; APNs keeps only one pending notification per app for an offline device either way.

quiz.question: Your server sends a notification and the platform answers with an error saying the token is unregistered. What should the server do?
options: Retry with exponential backoff until the send succeeds.
Switch the message to high priority and send it again.
Keep the token and try again after the next app release.
Delete the token and stop sending to it.
quiz.explanation: An unregistered or invalid token is a permanent failure: the app was removed or the token replaced. Retrying and raising priority cannot help and only waste calls. The app will send its new token when it registers again.

quiz.question: A banking app sends a push 'You received a payment' with the amount only inside the notification. The user's phone was offline longer than the time to live. What is the design flaw?
options: The time to live should have been set to zero so the push is retried.
The amount should be fetched from the API when the app opens, since a push can be dropped.
Banking apps should not use push notifications at all, for any purpose.
The push should use a collapse key so the platform stores it longer.
quiz.explanation: A push is best effort and can expire without any signal. The payment itself must be available from the API, so the app shows it when opened, and the notification only draws the user's attention. A longer hold or a collapse key does not make delivery guaranteed.
